(1/3) As its season of giving, our

 report today is free for everyone. Would be remiss to not make our thoughts public given we one of few with unique background to tackle this new corporate governance debate with no conflicts of interest. This is 11 pages of baby!

(2/3) 
$LULU
: All This Board Intrigue Can Drive A Person Lulu At one point in my life, I thought Kevin Plank (founder 
$UAA
) was the king of narrative generation, but it would seem Chip Wilson (founder Lululemon) has surpassed him by a mile. Chip has practically refined his image into a modern day “Rocky” story by now and everybody (in the all-important Americas segment of Lululemon) likes an underdog that’s been training for over a decade to take out the status quo. Nobody cares about the massive shareholder value delivered by Calvin McDonald, all the current Board seems to hear is “Rocky, Rocky, Rocky”. That’s kind of the problem here. It’s one thing to set high level strategy (which is what the Board does) and it’s another thing to execute that strategy (which is what CEOs do). Outsiders really don’t know where the failure is, but as we discuss in this note, the Board has largely boxed themselves in on this topic. We are almost certain Chip has been waiting on the sidelines for this one moment, but he is correct to question the current situation in our opinion. This note is unusual as we dig deeply into the corporate governance of Lululemon. We assess the slate of directors proposed by Chip, which quite frankly seem highly difficult to find much fault with on surface level. We look at the activist Elliott and seriously wonder why of all people they seem to think that Jane Nielsen should lead a company that most would agree has a product problem. But most importantly, we talk about the current Board of Lululemon, where there surprisingly are a lot of perspectives from the consumer staples world for a consumer discretionary company. However, we also find it a bit confusing how an $11 billion revenue company with positive revenue growth and 20% EBIT margins (despite tariffs) is the new definition of “weak” (according to the current market narrative), especially when they are still gaining market share. The potential Lululemon stock timeline that we proposed in our September note remains somewhat on track. The only difference is the unforeseen proxy war that Chip hinted at and then proceeded to subsequently launch since we last wrote. That got the sell-side upgrade cycle happening a bit earlier than expected (particularly with super bears) but there is a long way to go on that topic. We had previously hoped for Jonathan Cheung to be at the upcoming ICR meetings but at this point investors deserve a chance to meet Andre Maestrini since they almost certainly won’t be meeting Marti Morfitt (Chairwoman) – probably the person Chip is most directly going after. Highly recommend that she also does some investor meetings like the one I personally hosted in Boston when Glenn Murphy (former Chairman, CEO Gap, etc) managed a similar transition. We continue to believe the reasonable range of EPS outcomes this year is $12.75 to $13.40 (same range as our note from September). We also continue to believe there is a significantly wide range of potential outcomes in 2026, although we are incrementally warming up to the more optimistic scenarios. This simply represents the front summary of our 11 page report. You can find the entire report for free at our website (link in profile but also in post #3). We wish everybody an amazing 2026 to come!

But after digging into the numbers, Cignetti might still be the most undervalued coach in college football (and not for the reason you might think). We all know what Cignetti has done at IU is remarkable — he turned a perennial cellar-dweller into the national championship favorite just two years after his arrival. This has transformed IU's athletic department: • Before the 2025 season even kicked off, ticket revenue for IU's football team had surpassed $13 million. • Indiana announced a $50 million stadium naming rights deal with Merchants Bank. • Fundraising has hit a record high, with billionaire IU alum Mark Cuban donating to the athletic department for the first time ever. But that's the obvious stuff; Cignetti's real impact comes in the admissions office. IU's football team is essentially a marketing vehicle for the university — 24 million people watched them win the Rose Bowl, 18 million watched them win the Big Ten Championship, and when College Gameday visited Indiana's campus last year, more than 2 million people watched a 3-hour commercial about the school. This publicity is worth hundreds of millions of dollars and is having a real impact on Indiana's finances. In 2025 alone, Indiana University set school records for total enrollment (48,626 students), freshman class size (10,127 students), first-year out-of-state students (4,697), and application volume (73,400). Indiana University Applicants • 2019-20: 44,178 • 2020-21: 46,623 • 2021-22: 50,159 • 2022-23: 54,345 • 2023-24: 67,731 • 2024-25: 73,400 But since IU can only admit so many students each year, they leverage the additional demand to 1) rotate the composition of their student body toward out-of-state students, and 2) become more selective academically. Out-of-state students now account for about 50% of IU's total enrollment, with the school admitting a total of 4,697 new out-of-state students in 2025 — roughly 500 more out-of-state students than IU's previous record. This is an important distinction because out-of-state students pay $30,000 more in annual tuition – $12,000 for Indiana residents versus $42,000 for non-residents. 500 new out-of-state students x $30,000 tuition difference ––––––––– = $15 million annually If you multiply that by a four-year degree, these out-of-state students are worth $60 million more to IU than their in-state counterparts. And since football success attracts more applicants, IU's admissions office can be more selective. Indiana's Fall 2025 class had a median high school GPA of 3.94 — the highest in IU admissions history. This creates a virtuous cycle. Better sports → more applicants → better students → higher rankings. Higher rankings then lead to even more applicants, and, eventually, higher tuition revenues. This is exactly what happened at Alabama with Nick Saban, and it's a big reason why Indiana is completely comfortable giving Cignetti new contracts every year. P.S. Year 7 of Covid. My mother needed to return a final sale item. In store returns only for final sale items. I also had a gift card I wanted to use. So we went to the mall outside New Orleans. A known respiratory illness hotspot right now. I used to love malls. I don’t anymore. I have Long Covid. And over time, my body learned something my mind didn’t ask for. I can feel it when Covid is nearby. When someone is infected. Not anxiety. Not imagination. A physical alarm. I was fine in the car. Fine walking in. Then I stepped into the Lululemon dressing room. I just needed to make sure the shirt fit before I spent my gift card. Instant nose itch. Pressure flooding my ears. Eyes burning. That familiar warning. I rushed frantically, hands shaking, pulling fabric over my head. It fit. I needed to leave. As I stepped out, I heard it. A woman coughing hard. Wet. Uncontrolled. Standing inches away, browsing leggings like nothing was wrong. That’s where the warning I had came from I assumed nervously. Later, passing the food court, I turned my head to look. It was packed. And my vision became blurred. Eyes on fire burning. Vertigo hit so hard I almost collapsed. Nose screaming with the tingly itching. We moved fast to get by. The last hit came in line for coffee. I planned on bringing the coffee out to the car to enjoy it on the way home. The back of my throat started burning and felt dry and scratchy. Ears became full again. That awful question looping in my mind as my eyes scanned the area: Who is it? Who is infected here? We made it back to the car. We escaped. I began to enjoy my coffee. But I miss the old world. I miss not being able to panic everywhere I go. Covid didn’t just take health. It took safety away in ordinary places. I live inside a body that no longer trusts the world. It listens constantly. It detects danger while others feel nothing. There is no true rest for me. Only the tension of waiting for the next invisible threat to pass close enough to trigger the alarm. What people call a 6th sense is not a gift to me. It’s a survival reflex burned into me by repeated harm. A curse that wakes with me, walks with me, and never sleeps. Even when I desperately need it to.

In the 2010s, Lululemon turned its $100 black stretchy leggings into a status symbol and the foundation of a fast-growing new category with a corny name: athleisure. Over the course of a decade, women traded their jeans for leggings and men traded their khakis for stretchy pants. Lululemon expanded at a breakneck pace, racking up more than $10 billion in annual sales with 796 stores and 39,000 employees. But in 2024, Lululemon’s sales growth started to slow, and by 2025, sales actually shrank in its most important market, North America. As Levi’s and Gap boasted about the comeback of jeans in wider, looser styles, it was clear Lululemon was not simply overstretched but uncool. Just look online, where a million little competitors are stealing Lululemon’s customers. Alo is for West Village girls and their followers. Adanola is for Ssense shoppers who are done with Alo. Gymshark is for lifters who drink creatine. Vuori is for networking in Marin County. Set Active is for 20-somethings who love Parke. And for everyone else? The budget shoppers with influencer fatigue? Now, every place from Quince and Old Navy to Costco sells decent leggings and sweatpants, and searches for “Y2K activewear” are spiking on eBay. As Lululemon strains for a new identity and its copycat competitors jostle for clout, athleisure needs a kick in the pants. Because at this point, how many more leggings can we buy? Podcast Summary | Call Her Daddy: Sarah J Maas: The Wait Is Over Overview Sarah J. Maas, author of the massively popular Throne of Glass, A Court of Thorns and Roses, and Crescent City series, details her journey from a discouraged teenage writer to a literary powerhouse with over 75 million books sold. She reveals the profound personal traumas, including a traumatic emergency C-section and a mental health crisis, that have directly shaped her narratives, moving beyond the "smut" label to explore themes of survival, empowerment, and authentic female experience. Maas asserts complete creative control over her work, from rejecting compromise in future adaptations to defying publishing norms with her upcoming, uniquely structured ACOTAR releases, framing success as the freedom to tell her stories exactly as she envisions them. Key Themes - Creative control is non-negotiable for Maas, who views adaptations as core to her legacy and will reject any changes made for demographic appeal or that deviate from her vision. - Her writing is a channeled, emotional process where she physically embodies her characters, with major plotlines and character arcs emerging directly from her personal trauma, therapy, and growth. - She intentionally writes authentic, relatable fantasy for women by including "the real stuff" like bodily functions and complex motherhood, rejecting the dismissal of her work as "just smut" as a sexist double standard. - Maas’s career is a story of defiant independence, overcoming near-universal early rejection and discouragement from family and academia to build a universe where her series now converge as planned. - Success is defined as creative freedom and personal happiness, not just sales, with a mindset focused on long-term storytelling on her own terms rather than external validation. Detailed Summary Sarah J. Maas writes from a personal, joyful space in her bedroom at a tidy desk adorned with crystals and a Lululemon bag. Her process involves specific rituals, like requiring three coasters for different drinks and snacking on Flamin’ Hot Cheetos. Inspiration comes from soundtracks played on vinyl, including the 2022 "Batman" score and music from "Demon Slayer." This controlled environment fuels a writing method she describes as almost supernatural, where plot elements align as if from a "humanwide psychic thing" and she physically cries while channeling her characters' emotions. Her path to this point was fiercely independent. As a teenager, she shifted from assigned "boring" school books to self-discovered fantasy, a passion she kept secret alongside an anime love for Sailor Moon. She began writing Throne of Glass at 16 on floppy disks using a square iMac as an escape from an unhappy high school experience. Despite material support from her lawyer parents, including an unlimited book budget, they were skeptical of her publishing prospects. This discouragement was echoed by a creative writing MFA director who visibly dismissed her for writing fantasy. Maas resisted all traditional literary training, insisting on writing her chosen genre from the start. This defiance shaped her career. She faced near-universal rejection, with every agent and publisher except one initially saying no. She wrote the first two ACOTAR books in about two months in 2008 while waiting for responses on Throne of Glass. Crescent City began as a private, unpublished passion project for creative play, featuring more cursing, with no initial plan to publish. All three major series were designed to converge, a complex architecture developed over many years starting very early in her career. Maas strongly rejects the reductive label of "smut" or "romantic fantasy." She argues this is a sexist double standard where any inclusion of sexuality by women authors leads to the devaluation of their entire work. For her, sexual content is "intensely tied to their own emotional journeys" and character development. She points to fans who credit A Court of Mist and Fury with inspiring them to leave abusive relationships, not just for the "hot scenes." She intentionally writes "the real stuff," including bodily functions like periods, to create authentic, relatable fantasy worlds for women. This authenticity is rooted in deep personal experience. Her traumatic emergency C-section with her son, who was two weeks late and in distress, left lasting physical and emotional scars. The incision was made "way too high" and "destroyed like the flow and look of my stomach." A male doctor yelled at her for eating before the procedure, and only a med school intern showed her kindness. She believes she and her son would have died a century earlier. A later gynecologist reacted with anger to the scar, calling it "unnecessary" and the result of a "lazy" doctor. This trauma directly fed into the emotional core of Feyre's pregnancy storyline, focusing on loss of bodily autonomy. Motherhood as a source of strength and complexity, not a glossed-over "happily ever after," became a key theme. Writing A Court of Silver Flames was intertwined with her own mental health crisis in fall 2019, which involved prolonged panic attacks and a "very dark place" that led her to therapy and medication. She wrote Nesta's emotional arc while actively processing her own trauma; the pivotal scene where Nesta breaks down on a hike was conceived during Maas's own emotional breakdown on a hike in New Zealand. Therapy helped her separate self-worth from professional success. Her therapist had her mentally walk through a scenario where her career was "all done" to prove she would survive. This allowed her to reclaim joy in writing, which had become a stressful "job" due to deadlines, leading to panic attacks. She views her family, husband, and friends as unconditional blessings that "nothing can take away." Her character dynamics often emerge organically. When first writing ACOTAR, she did not plan the plot; the character Rhysand entered a scene unexpectedly, changing the story's direction. She finds irony in early fans getting tattoos of Tamlin before his full controlling arc was revealed. She views Tamlin's behavior as a result of trauma and lack of emotional tools, not pure villainy, but does not excuse actions like locking Feyre in the manor. She is conflicted about a potential redemption arc, weighing narrative exploration against validating readers who saw their own abusive relationships in him. Maas believes characters in relationships must maintain autonomy and equality, a non-negotiable principle. She intentionally writes main characters like Rhysand to make serious mistakes from a place of love and fear, creating realistic conflict. Rhysand's failure to fully communicate the risks of Feyre's pregnancy is framed as a "bad call" made from terror, informed by his inexperience despite being over 500 years old. The most romantic moment between them, the Starfall scene, was inspired by Florence and the Machine's "Cosmic Love." Chapter 55 of Silver Flames is cited as a major emotional release, a culmination of long-built backstory that required little editing. The concept of "mates" in her series explores the tension between biological destiny and free will. She finds the tension of an unwanted bond a compelling challenge. The next ACOTAR book is confirmed for release on October 27th, noting it took time due to personal life events and finding the right story. This upcoming story defies traditional publishing. It is one massive narrative split into four parts, with Part 1 alone at approximately 400 pages. The full story is over a thousand pages across three physical volumes. The first part releases October 27th, with the next installment (Parts 2 & 3 combined) on January 12th. This back-to-back schedule is to avoid making fans wait. The project was written quickly after a creative block broke during a stay in Montana. She is currently editing two massive books simultaneously, prioritizing the organic needs of the story over industry rules. Looking forward, Maas asserts complete creative control over any future TV or film adaptations, rejecting changes made for demographic appeal. She will not compromise on casting, citing an ongoing search for the "perfect" actor for a character like Rhysand. She has reclaimed the rights to all her literary works, a significant professional shift. She defines success as the creative freedom to tell stories on her own terms combined with personal happiness. She maintains a long-term mindset, originally willing to publish even one book in her lifetime. She rejects external doubt as motivation, responding to being told she "couldn't do something" with a defiant "Watch me." On series futures, she confirms Bryce and Hunt from Crescent City are endgame, dismissing fan theories about Bryce and Azriel. A Throne of Glass book project was set aside as it required more time than currently available. She has 3-4 unpublished full books for different series on her computer that may never be released. She included otters in Crescent City simply because she loves them. Her fan interactions remain deeply personal; she often approaches readers in public to thank them and sometimes interrupts their reading to discuss the book, viewing the connection as the ultimate reward for her defiant, authentic, and emotionally charged creative journey. The growth of my social media account and root of my legitimacy is purely in the fact that I know how the ruling classes in Britain, Italy, and the United States dressed during the 20th century. When Vivek Ramaswamy and Pete Hegseth wear tan shoes with navy suits, I can say "this looks like shit to most people because it's not how King Charles and Gianni Agenlli would have dressed." When Kash Patel puts contrast buttonholes on his suits, I can say it's wrong because the ruling classes across these countries during that period would have never chosen such a thing. You read this as legitimate purely because you accept the legitimacy of these classes in forming our sense of aesthetics. Someone who has no interest in these classes — such as Paul Harden and Yohji Yamamoto — rightly disregards all of these notions and makes tailoring according to different rules. The polo shirt is no different. The spread of the polo shirt is a story about how a pullover garment migrated from the polo fields played by British imperialists to tennis legends in France and eventually to the golfing middle classes in the United States. This is entirely a story about race, class, and gender. Football jerseys and basketball shorts don't enjoy such history, and thus they are not seen as legitimate business clothes. This is an email mistake any ecommerce brand can make easily, without even noticing. Here's how to not end up like LululemonLululemon was fined for sending marketing emails without an unsubscribe link. In most countries, the law differentiates between "marketing" and "transactional" emails. Transactional emails include important information like receipts, order confirmations, etc. Whereas marketing emails pitch products and promotions. Popular ecommerce ESPs (like Klaviyo) sometimes DO NOT include unsubscribe links in transactional emails by default (in many cases, unsubscribe links are only legally required for marketing emails). Based on the article, it appears Lululemon put "marketing content" into their "transactional" emails. That's what exposed them to the fines. Had they sent the exact same content in a separate marketing automation where their ESP included the unsubscribe link, the same content would have been sent legally.

Textile Robot Skin Turns Fabric into a Nervous System Robot skin is getting touchier. The Chinese company JQ Industries just introduced a fabric-based electronic skin (e-skin) to give robots a humanlike sense of touch. Made from plant-derived materials, it behaves like fabric and can bend and conform like clothing without restricting movement. So basically, Lululemon with embedded sensors. The skin is woven with conductive fibers that detect pressure, contact and force distribution. The system uses sensor gloves for the hands and pressure-sensing soles for the feet. The E-skin acts as a distributed nervous system. It transmits data from thousands of sensing points to the robot’s artificial intelligence for instant decision-making. It integrates with simulation environments like NVIDIA Isaac Sim and MuJoCo for training AI models using tactile feedback. Shanghai-based JQ Industries demonstrated the capabilities using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, but the technology is intended for use across platforms. The company says the enhanced sensitivity unlocks more precise grip control and better handling of delicate objects. They say it also makes robots safer around humans. JQ’s ultimate goal is to create a closed loop so next-gen robots can learn from touch the same way humans do. JQ says its technology differs from traditional electronic skin that relies on delicate thin film that’s hard to produce and tends to degrade with bending. It’s produced with textile manufacturing techniques like modified industrial weaving and roll-to-roll production. Launched in early 2024, JQ Industries operates as Weihai Juqiao Industrial Technology. The early-stage startup is scaling production of the tactile-sensing technology with at least $2.8 million raised to date.

B) Along similar lines, some research would suggest there may be a case of pluralistic ignorance here, where board members on a cohesive, comfortable board that lacks the right diversity may individually perceive the need for more change, yet jointly underestimate the others' perceived need for strategic change, resulting in consensus around lukewarm strategic decisions that do not go far enough. C) Boards with long-tenured directors, and directors with similar background, capabilities, and social capital work better for mature, stable, well-performing firms, which doesn't seem to be the case here. Can We Admit That Low IQ People Exist? There are different classes of people. Different cognitive bands. Different capabilities. Some are smarter, some are simpler. They tend to congregate into groups. Saying this out loud makes you a monster, but I'm saying it because we all know it’s true. And it is: IQ distributions are bell curves. The middle of the curve, the part most of us live in, sits between roughly 85 and 115. About two-thirds of people are in there. The other third splits into the tails. One tail noticeably below the middle, one tail noticeably above. The shape of the curve is not contested. The honesty about what it means is contested. I worked this out at Meatstock - a meat festival that tours Australia, and a ‘Destruction Derby’ at a rural racetrack. I’m talking about authentic events, in rural environments. Not your typical urban show where the country comes to the city. A different sort of human goes to these rural shows. Meatstock came to Lardner Park, an hour and a half southeast of Melbourne. It’s an open plains area, the kind of paddock that runs cattle eleven months of the year and trade shows on the twelfth. The Sydney version of Meatstock runs at Olympic Park: modern, urban, and surrounded by professionals living in medium density townhouses. The Melbourne version runs in a paddock, and the crowd it draws is not the crowd that turns up at Olympic Park. I rolled in wearing a 2XU tracksuit, thinking I was toning down my usual edgy athleisure style (Lululemon etc). I thought leaving the Volvo XC40 at home and taking the Ford Ranger with the bull bar and all terrains was not just a wise weather and terrain choice but would also help me fit in. To appear less of a city slicker. Turns out, my tracksuit was too nice, my car was too shiny, and my brain was too high functioning. The thing is, I am not a city slicker. I farm. I run cattle. I spend all day tensioning barbed wire. I scrape cow poo off my face after it flings off tractor tyres and into my eyes. I know more about welding, farming, fencing and machinery than most people who walked past me at Meatstock and Destruction Derby. Many of them were neckbeards with a caravan. Their bodies screamed the evidence of a lifetime of sedentary video gaming and TV watching, not trades or farming. They must love meat as much as I do! Despite my efforts at dressing down, it wasn’t enough to fit in. I also had to translate myself: A singer-songwriter was singing on stage, performing a country song with a presentation that contradicted her lyrics, a pretty obvious artistic move. Sometimes her songs would back-to-back conflict with each other in psychological framing. Another fascinating insight inter her tapestry of personality and life experience. Other times she’d make typical stage-remarks we are all used to: ‘you’re singing so well’, despite nobody singing. Then she’d display remarkable authenticity and vulnerability by admitting to and owning errors wholeheartedly. What a captivating display of emotional and cognitive performance, tension and contradiction in real time! I wondered why she would cover over some things, and expose others. Did she want to signal transparency? Or polish? Or both – and why? What drove her in those fleeting moments of micro-decision? But I couldn't say a word about any of this. Not because the people around me would have disagreed. Because they would have been embarrassed. Can you imagine if I turned to the friendly neckbeard in the VB shirt next to me and remarked on the cognitive dissonance of the performer, wondering whether she was experiencing a fluctuating confidence state as her set unfolded? Would he even understand the concept of cognitive dissonance? Or was I simply revealing my prejudice, assuming his lower cognitive ability? It didn’t matter. I couldn’t take the chance. I believe the observation itself would have made him feel exposed. Stupid. Big words, big concepts, wholly inappropriate for the setting. So I held it all in. The same thing happened at the Destruction Derby I attended in a similar rural setting. There appeared to be some kind of uniform enforcement because everyone was wearing all black. Black jeans, black shirts, the occasional heavy metal or beer logo. Not charcoal. Not grey. No colour, no stripes, no patterns. Just solid black. And all the same – black jeans and hoodies. Maybe the local Kmart didn’t stock any other style. I overheard their conversations as we sat on the grass, with my highly paid and credentialed doctor friends, who attended with me. My wife heard them too, sitting in her classic sundress. We stuck out like we didn’t belong, because we didn’t. The banter I overheard proved as much. The things they said around me were not stupid, just visceral. Simple and without abstraction. They were running at full capacity in their register, open and authentic with their friends and family. Direct, grounded, and fluent but certainly not abstract. Not cognitively challenging. Not at all curious, just statements of observation and fact. Never a question. At both Meatstock and at Destruction Derby, I was the one shedding cognitive load to fit in and meet everyone where they were at. And I had to shed a lot. This is the part nobody wants to admit. There are different classes. There are different cognitive bands. The people I was around genuinely could not have processed an abstraction about staging psychology or daytime-versus-nighttime audience framing, or fashion semiotics. I was certain they didn’t notice their communal uniform and the group dynamics that it forces, especially when someone fails to comply. But I did. Not because they are lazy or undereducated. They may be those things – I don’t know – but more critically is that a cognitive operation isn't one they run in their head. They run others. They run trucks, they run brisket pits, they run fencing rigs and chainsaws and welding gear. They run social cues and hierarchies unconsciously, and probably claim them to be ‘self-evident’. Except they’re not self-evident. Just like any other human group or class, they were taking part in a sociological ritual, their decision making shunted toward particular paths. And here's the move most people make, and the move I refuse to make: Most people, having admitted the cognitive gap, immediately reach for a balancing equation: ‘Sure, they can't think like me, a lawyer, but I can't milk a cow, so…’ This is a cheap admission. It's pity dressed as humility. It pretends the two capabilities are equivalent, that the ledger balances out, that nobody is actually behind on anything because we're all just specialists. That’s not true. And that's not what I saw. I saw that they were genuinely behind in abstraction and cognitive depth. Genuinely. And it doesn’t matter, but not for the weak reason I just explained some people reach for. It doesn’t matter because their worth doesn't rest on it. Worth is not stored in cognitive horsepower. Worth is not stored in earning potential or vocabulary range or analytical capacity, or urban worldliness. It's stored somewhere else entirely. In being made, in being human, in being here. The capability gap is real but the worth gap is not. The problem comes when you notice a capability difference and then erroneously conclude that you are ‘better’ than someone else. That you are worth more than they are. You’re not. Once you can hold both ledgers separately, the whole tension relaxes. You can look at someone genuinely less cognitively able than you, poorer than you, less experienced than you, less aware than you, and still not need to flatter them, rebalance the ledger, or manufacture a counter-skill that proves they're really your equal. In some domains, they are not your equal. In fact, cumulatively, they might be objectively less useful than you. They may be less intelligent than you. They may be less valuable to the capitalist system than you. Their entire table of talents may be smaller than yours. But that still doesn’t touch their dignity, moral worth, right to a vote and a voice (no matter how uneducated). I really enjoyed Meatstock and the Destruction Derby. I enjoyed the conversations with stall holders and the guy who won the award for best mullet. Top bloke. Sure, I had to park my brain for most of the day but accepting that this was a realm I would never be understood in, and our minds would never meet, was a relief. Maybe I’m smarter than them. I don’t know. Maybe they’re ‘physically’ smarter than me, at practical things. I don’t know. It doesn’t matter. I’m not balancing the ledger anymore. I’m telling the truth. Low IQ people exist. "You get rich by betting on things other people are wrong about." I did a Zoom with the students in my course last week. One guy said he wanted to buy a duplex in Santa Fe. He told me the numbers; they sounded great. But then he said his whole family was protesting the neighborhood. "Why would you want to own there?" Problem is, his family is thinking about their personal preferences, not about investments. They're playing a different game. They're thinking about the Lululemon and the Panera Bread, not the Class B with a 6% cap rate. I went through the same thing when I started buying properties. Everyone protested that it's a bad idea. The objections fell along three lines. 1: They were worried about an impending market crash because they were all hopped up on recency bias. 2: They objected I didn't know anything about construction; I had no blue collar background. I came from a family that cherished academia with a near-religious zeal. (Ironically, the bastion of critical thinking was the one thing they never thought critically about.) They urged me to stick to my studies; stay in my lane. 3: They objected to the choice of neighborhood because they thought it was "dangerous," despite having never studied the local crime maps, never having spent afternoons at local establishments, never having conversed with a few dozen of the residents. They had neither quantitative nor qualitative data, but they decided it was "dangerous" and wrote it off as such. I knew they were wrong, but it took an enormous level of confidence to move forward, because I was young and untested, and had never really defied my family like that. Thank goodness I did. That single decision is the reason that I now am the most financially successful person in my family (by a wide margin). I knew they were wrong, and I bet accordingly. Even when I had very little to bet. Even when I was living with five roommates, driving a 10-year-old Camry, buying groceries from Costco, wearing thrift store clothes, and never going to restaurants. I had almost nothing, but I bet it all, because I believed in my so-called "thesis," although I didn't think of it like that at the time. I just thought of it as an opportunity that I couldn't pass up. So don't listen to the people who tell you not to. Because if you do, then 15 years later, you'll end up just as broke as they still are. If everyone knew how to make money, then they would. Most people don't know how, and their well-meaning advice will lead you astray. And that's why you get rich by betting on things that other people are wrong about. By the time they recognize the opportunity in hindsight, they'll say, "Wow, you sure did get lucky."

That is the cleanest way to read the Chip Wilson proxy fight: not nostalgia, not founder drama, but a live fight over who gets to define the brand now. Lululemon is urging holders to reject Wilson’s director slate — Marc Maurer, Laura Gentile and Eric Hirshberg — and back its own nominees, Chip Bergh, Esi Eggleston Bracey and Teri List. The board’s message is blunt: Wilson’s perspective is outdated, his campaign is damaging, and putting his nominees in the room would weaken the board and disrupt the incoming CEO’s plan. Wilson is attacking the one thing the market actually pays for. His case is that LULU has drifted from the core consumer and needs sharper merchandising, better store execution, and more spending behind marketing and product development. That is not a random activist checklist. For a premium consumer stock, brand heat is the asset, and when that starts leaking, the P&L usually sees it after the customer already has. His nominees fit that critique: On Holding, ESPN, Activision — less “audit committee polish,” more brand, product, media and consumer engagement. The catch: founder instinct is not the same thing as governance. A founder can be directionally right about the brand and still be the wrong mechanism for public-company control. That is where Lululemon is pressing. The company says settlement talks collapsed after Wilson pushed for three directors of his choosing, including two immediate appointments, plus quarterly meetings with the new CEO. That shifts the question from “does Wilson see the problem?” to “is this a board refresh or a control campaign?” The board has its own credibility issue. It is asking investors to trust the current plan at the exact moment Wilson is arguing the plan already missed the consumer. That is a hard sell if execution does not improve quickly. For shareholders, this is not a clean founder-good, board-bad story. It is a tradeoff between creative aggression and operational stability during a CEO transition. Wilson wants disruption because he thinks stability became complacency. The board wants stability because it thinks disruption could damage the very brand he claims to protect. Bottom line: LULU’s proxy fight is a premium-brand duration test. The winner will not be the side with the better press release. It will be the side that proves it can recover brand heat without breaking the machine.

While waiting for his drink, he casually mentioned to the barista that he was “taking some time between exits.” The barista nodded sympathetically, the way one might respond to news of a difficult divorce. “Oh wow,” she said. “Good for you.” The other thing nobody prepares you for about Palo Alto is how offensively healthy everyone appears to be. You arrive thinking you’re doing reasonably well. Maybe you’ve had a salad recently. Maybe you took a walk on purpose once. Then suddenly you’re standing in line behind a man who is allegedly fifty-two years old but looks like he was assembled in a Scandinavian laboratory last Thursday. Everyone here has the skin of a newborn dolphin. Women in black Lululemon glide past carrying green juice and somehow manage to look both relaxed and aggressively optimized. Men who claim to have “just been slammed with board meetings” still possess the compact musculature of professional cyclists fleeing the Tour de France. Even the dogs look expensive and emotionally regulated. Back home, if you saw a group of middle-aged men jogging shirtless, you assumed there’d been some sort of emergency. Here they travel in organized clusters at six in the morning discussing mitochondrial health and seed oils. One man at Coupa told me he’d “fully eliminated inflammatory inputs.” I didn’t ask what this meant because I was eating banana bread and suddenly felt ashamed. Everywhere I looked, there were men in fleece vests speaking a language that sounded vaguely English but contained no recognizable human emotion. “We’re building tooling around decentralized trust.” “The space is evolving super fast.” “There’s a lot of energy around synthetic cognition.” One man said, “I’m not optimizing for money anymore.” He said this while sitting in front of a laptop that cost four thousand dollars. I rented a tiny apartment near Stanford University and quickly learned that Stanford students travel in packs like very confident gazelles. They move at dangerous speeds on electric scooters while discussing whether consciousness can be uploaded to the cloud. One afternoon, I overheard two undergraduates talking outside the bookstore. “I’m only taking four classes this quarter because my startup’s scaling.” The other one nodded solemnly. “Yeah, burnout is real.” They both looked about fourteen years old. The strangest thing about Palo Alto is that everyone appears to be either: 1. starting a company, 2. selling a company, 3. investing in a company, or 4. recovering emotionally from being insufficiently early to Bitcoin. Even the children seem busy. At a playground near downtown, I heard a father say to his toddler: “Sweetie, use your words. Are you feeling pre-product-market-fit?” The child burst into tears, which honestly felt appropriate. At lunch, people migrate toward Nobu Palo Alto with the determination of spawning salmon. I went there once with a friend who works in venture capital, a profession I still don’t fully understand except that it seems to involve eating expensive sushi while rejecting other people’s dreams. The hostess asked if we had a reservation. My friend smiled. “We know Kevin.” This turned out to be sufficient. Inside, every table contained a conversation that sounded medically concerning. “Our runway’s getting tighter.” “We may need another round.” “He’s pivoting hard.” It was impossible to tell whether these people were discussing startups or emergency aviation procedures. I once met a venture capitalist there who casually informed me he was sixty-one. I laughed because I thought he was joking. He wasn’t. The man looked like a substitute Peloton instructor. His jawline could have sliced sashimi. During dinner he ate approximately four molecules of tuna and spent twenty minutes explaining the anti-inflammatory benefits of Nordic sauna cycles. “I’ve completely cut out alcohol,” he said. Then, after a pause: “Except ceremonial mezcal.” At one point my friend leaned over and whispered, “That’s Sam Altman.” I looked across the room and saw a pale man in a gray sweater drinking sparkling water while listening very intensely. “But that could also just be somebody from product,” I said. “That’s true,” my friend admitted. Celebrity sightings here are uniquely disappointing because everyone already looks like a tech billionaire. Half the men dress like they’ve been evacuated from an REI store. The other half look like they’re on their way to testify before Congress. Once, at Whole Foods, I became convinced I had seen Elon Musk examining avocados. I stared for nearly thirty seconds before realizing it was simply an exhausted father wearing a black jacket and the expression of someone trying to colonize Mars while also remembering to buy oat milk. The social rules here are baffling. People don’t ask where you’re from. They ask: “What are you working on?” And when you answer honestly — “Oh, I’m writing essays” — they react the way Victorians might respond to hearing you collect human teeth. At parties, conversations become competitive in very specific ways. In normal cities, people brag about vacations or home renovations. In Palo Alto, people brag about suffering. “I haven’t slept in three days.” “I forgot to eat yesterday.” “I accidentally took two investor calls during my anniversary dinner.” Everyone laughs proudly, like overworked raccoons. The host introduced me to a man who was “doing fascinating work in longevity.” The man looked thirty-five. “I’m actually fifty-eight,” he said. There was a long silence while everyone calculated whether eternal life might be worth hearing the phrase “biohacking journey” every day forever. Around dessert, someone asked if I’d tried cold plunging. I said no. Another guest looked genuinely alarmed. “But then how do you regulate inflammation?” I almost answered, “Catholic guilt,” but I didn’t think they’d understand. There is an exhausting amount of intentionality around the human body here. People don’t merely exercise; they “train for longevity.” They don’t eat lunch; they “optimize glucose response.” A friend invited me to breakfast and then consumed what appeared to be damp bark in a ceramic bowl. “This changed my biomarkers,” he told me. Everyone has some combination of: * personal trainer * sleep consultant * infrared sauna * standing desk * cold plunge * emotional-support electrolyte packet Meanwhile I eat one blueberry muffin and immediately look like Winston Churchill. The local gym frightened me so badly I canceled my membership after one visit. One guy casually mentioned he’d just completed an ultramarathon. Another said: “Oh nice, which one?” As if there were several. I once tried jogging around the Stanford campus and was immediately overtaken by a woman pushing a stroller uphill while calmly discussing a seed-round valuation on AirPods. The stroller contained twins. The twins were eating organic almond butter from reusable bamboo pouches. One of them looked more emotionally resilient than I am. And despite all this optimization, everyone also seems profoundly exhausted. You’ll see some radiant-looking founder with perfect posture and suspiciously white teeth saying things like: “I haven’t slept in four days.” Or: “My WHOOP data says I’m technically deceased.” It creates a strange atmosphere where nobody appears to age normally. The entire town feels suspended in a permanent state of highly funded wellness panic. By midnight, everyone at the Atherton dinner party had become extremely earnest. A venture capitalist explained to me that artificial intelligence would soon eliminate the need for most human labor. “What will people do all day?” I asked. He shrugged. “Found podcasts, probably.” Later, walking home through silent streets full of Teslas charging like sleeping livestock, I passed a young man talking very intensely into his phone. “No, listen,” he said. “It’s Uber, but for emotions.” And the terrible thing was, part of me thought: That’ll probably get funded.”

$EOS.AX If you scroll my profile, you would think I like to do TA. But actually I love doing fundamental analysis as well. I enjoy finding gems and digging through the company just as much as I enjoy the TA. That work takes weeks, and I'm super selective, that's why I don't spam tickers continuously. But when I do put out a thesis, you can bet that I have done the homework. Here is my framework: Question zero: enabler or beneficiary? Before anything else. Does this company build the foundation of the AI buildout, or just use AI to improve a service? Enablers are examples like semis, memory, neoclouds, photonics. The picks and shovels. Beneficiaries are fintech, SaaS, healthcare. Enablers capture the most value right now because they can't be skipped. Demand is outstripping supply. The odds of picking a winner are higher. Beneficiaries fight in crowded markets, and at worst AI eats them. See the recent SaaS bloodbath. Pick enablers to be included in your portfolio want enablers. 1. Leadership. Everything about a company stems from the top, the culture, the finances, the engineering, the technology, the customer relations etc. > Does the founder have experience that actually maps to this company, or a resume from an unrelated field? > How long has the CEO been in the seat? > Is it founder led? > Do they own real stock, and are they buying in the open market or quietly selling? > Any history of missing their own guidance, related party deals, or restatements? And if so, why? Unproven at this scale is fine if the credentials fit and their own money is on the line. Documented dishonesty is an instant fail. 2. Revenue Quality. > Is it recurring, or a one time lump that won't repeat? > Is it spread across many customers, or does one whale carry the whole number and could walk tomorrow? > Where does it come from geographically? One country, or many? Heavy China exposure is a different risk than a diversified base across the US, Europe and Asia. > Does the cash flowing in match the revenue being booked, or is the growth living on paper? 3. Revenue Growth. This is crucial for finding 10 baggers > Is there a credible inflection coming, or just a steady trailing rate? > Is the capex already in the ground to support it? If not there are dilution risks. > Is the customer pipeline named, or hand waved? > Is there any guidance on revenue growth given by management? A flat company with a real inflection ahead beats a steady grower with nothing coming. 4. Moat. The edge that protects them. Extremely important to find winners in the long run as well. > Is it an artificial moat, the Lululemon or Nike kind, built on brand and marketing that a competitor can erode with enough spend? Or is it something only this company can do? > Switching costs, multi year qualification cycles, patents, sole supplier status? > Has anyone with money and reputation on the line validated it? A named hyperscaler, a platform leader, a strategic investor on the board? > External validators are hard evidence, not narrative. Counterparties don't sign off on weak operators. 5. Asymmetry. Risk to reward at today's price. Most people get this backwards. It is not "the stock has run, I missed it." It's "does the upside still pay me for the downside." > What's my floor? Cash on the balance sheet, trust value, book value? > If the bear case hits, how far do I actually fall? > If the thesis works, where does it go? > Does the probability weighted upside still beat the downside by a wide margin? A stock that has 5x'd and still pays you 2 to 1 is more asymmetric than one that has done nothing and pays you 1.3 to 1. There are many ways to value a company, for me, the best way to value growth stocks is looking at their forward earnings/revenues and comparing it to peers. This is what I did with 
$BRUN
 to determine it was undervalued. Find your style. 6. Conviction Gap. The space between what I can prove today and what the next catalysts will prove. > What is genuinely unknown right now? > Which way does the existing evidence lean? > What specific event would convert the unknown into fact? When does that event happen? A wide gap with evidence pointing the right way is the whole game. It means the market is pricing in uncertainty I have a reasoned view on. Thin analyst coverage isn't a red flag here. It's the opportunity. I write the bear case out in full and pick at it before I ever post. If I can't convince myself first, I won't try to convince you. To summarise 0. AI Enabler over beneficiary. 1. Leadership I trust. 2. Real revenue. 3. Forward growth. 4. A moat only they can build/is hard to replicate. 5. Asymmetry that pays me. 6. A gap with a catalyst to close it. You can take these 6 criteria to come up with a composite score to decide whether you want to decide to invest in the company or not. 7. How I integrate TA into all of this. The fundamentals tell me what to buy. The technicals tell me when. The best setup is when both line up. Great fundamentals with a broken chart just means you bag hold while you wait, sometimes for years even! See 
$PATH
. Arguably the right company, sadly the wrong tape. And this is huge opportunity cost. So once a name clears my framework, I check the chart for confluence. > Is the stock breaking out of a downtrend or a long consolidation? > Are the EMAs stacked bullish, shorter over longer, all sloping up? > Is there real volume driving the move, or is it drifting on nothing? Each one on its own may be noise, but stacked together, they can be a signal. That confluence is the difference between catching the entry and riding the wave, or being early and bleeding. Common take: Canadian companies don't buy from startups because they're risk-averse. I've sold to Canadian banks, retailers, grocers & pharmacy chains as a startup for 20 years. The description is accurate -- it really does suck to sell to Canadian businesses as a startup. But the reason is wrong. As a startup you're rarely selling just a solution -- you're selling a paradigm shift ("you run a custom ecommerce engine, but SaaS changes what's possible"). So the real ask is: adopt an unproven paradigm AND trust a small startup to deliver it. Now picture the typical Canadian buyer: a company that's rarely #1 in its field, comfortable in its position, with a decision-maker promoted on tenure -- not for being a maverick. The ones who DO take paradigm risks (Lululemon, Shopify) do it because reinvention is core to their identity. They're the exception. It's not that Canadian enterprises prefer US vendors. It's that if they're going to bet on a new paradigm, a small startup won't be the one to convince them -- but an OpenAI, SAP, or Salesforce will. There's something deeper underneath it too. Across art, science, and tech, Canadians rarely see themselves as the ones who define the next wave -- so they don't trust homegrown talent to do it either. We instinctively look elsewhere for the future.

Here's the actual list, organized by how "bootstrapped" they really were — there's a meaningful difference between "never took a dollar" and "raised one small round after proving the model." Tier 1: Never took venture capital (or took it only as a partial exit), reached $1B+ Mailchimp — Ben Chestnut and Dan Kurzius bootstrapped from a web design consultancy starting 2001. Sold to Intuit for $12B in 2021, largest bootstrapped exit ever. Never took outside investment. Zoho — Sridhar Vembu started in 1996, fully bootstrapped, ~$1.4B annual revenue with 100M+ users. Valued at ~$12.4B (2024 Hurun report). Has consistently turned down VC. Patagonia — Yvon Chouinard bootstrapped from selling climbing gear out of his car. Estimated $3B+ valuation; in 2022 transferred ownership to a trust dedicated to fighting climate change rather than selling or IPOing. Basecamp / 37signals — Jason Fried and DHH have been profitable for 25+ years, never took VC, multiple successful products. Founders' net worths in the hundreds of millions each; company valuation not public but estimates run $1B+. Craigslist — Craig Newmark deliberately kept the company lean. Estimated worth in the billions based on revenue (~$1B/year at peak), but he's resisted commercial expansion. Implied valuation easily $1B+. Valve — Gabe Newell self-funded with proceeds from his Microsoft stock. Estimated $10B+ valuation via Steam dominance. No outside investment. Epic Games — Tim Sweeney started in his parents' basement in 1991. Now valued at $30B+ after Fortnite. Took late strategic investment from Tencent and Sony, but the foundation was bootstrapped for ~20 years. Spanx — Sara Blakely started with $5,000 in savings in 2000. Bootstrapped for 21 years until Blackstone took majority in 2021 at $1.2B valuation. Blakely became a billionaire. Tier 2: Started with personal savings or credit cards (<$50K), eventually took VC after proving the model Atlassian — Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar started 2002 with $10K AUD on credit cards. No VC for 8 years and 40 consecutive profitable quarters. Now ~$40B market cap (NASDAQ: TEAM). Wayfair — Niraj Shah and Steve Conine started with $7K in 2002. Profitable in their first month, no VC until they hit $500M in revenue. Peak $40B, currently ~$6B post-correction. GitHub — Three co-founders bootstrapped from 2008-2012 before raising $100M from a16z. Sold to Microsoft for $7.5B in 2018. GoPro — Nick Woodman started with $10K from selling necklaces with his wife. IPO'd at $11B peak valuation, currently smaller after the action camera market commoditized. Yeti — Roy and Ryan Seiders bootstrapped from making fishing rods. IPO'd at $1.7B in 2018, currently ~$3B. Pluralsight — Aaron Skonnard bootstrapped for years before Insight Partners came in. Sold to Vista Equity for $3.5B in 2021. Calendly — Tope Awotona invested his life savings as part of a $550K seed round, remained capital-efficient for 7 years. Last valued at $3B in 2021. Shutterstock — Jon Oringer started with his own savings and his own photographs. Currently ~$2B market cap. SurveyMonkey — Ryan Finley bootstrapped from 1999, sold to Spectrum Equity in 2009. Was a unicorn at 2018 IPO, currently ~$1B+. Topgolf — Started bootstrapped 2000s, eventually took strategic investment. Now ~$4B+ as part of Topgolf Callaway. ZipRecruiter — Ian Siegel and team bootstrapped as a "lifestyle business" before raising $63M Series A. IPO'd 2021 at ~$2.4B, currently smaller. NerdWallet — Tim Chen bootstrapped 2009-2015 before $64M Series A. IPO'd 2021 around $1.3B. Campaign Monitor — Sydney-based, bootstrapped to scale before a $250M first round from Insight Venture Partners — the first-round size is the tell of how much they'd built on their own. Some legendary "almost bootstrapped" worth knowing: Lululemon — Chip Wilson started with personal savings in 1998. Now ~$35B market cap. Did some early strategic capital but no traditional VC path. Stripe — Often gets called bootstrapped but actually took early YC and angel funding (~$2M seed). Not strictly bootstrapped. WhatsApp — Took some early Sequoia investment but extremely capital-efficient. Sold to Facebook for $19B. Borderline. Patterns worth pulling out, given your serial-entrepreneur context: A few things this list reveals that's relevant for the ParkOS thinking: B2B SaaS dominates the truly bootstrapped tier. Mailchimp, Zoho, Atlassian, Basecamp, Calendly, Pluralsight, Campaign Monitor — recurring revenue businesses with low marginal cost are the most capital-efficient model in history. ParkOS fits this template structurally. The bootstrapped path consistently produces higher founder equity at exit. Wayfair's founders held substantial stakes at $40B peak. Atlassian's founders are still ~30% owners after IPO. Mailchimp's founders split $12B essentially intact. VC dilution typically leaves founders with 10-15% at IPO; bootstrappers often hold 40-70%+. The "no VC for X years" pattern is more common than "never any VC." Most of these companies eventually took some capital — but did so from a position of strength (already profitable, already at scale) which dramatically shifted the terms in founders' favor. The discipline is in when you take capital, not whether you ever do. Vertical-specific software + services (Yeti for outdoor, Spanx for shapewear, Patagonia for outdoor apparel) shows you don't need to be pure tech to bootstrap to billion-dollar scale. Operations-heavy businesses with strong brand equity work too. The clear common thread: all of these companies were profitable early and grew on customer revenue rather than investor capital. The VC playbook of "burn cash to grow then figure out unit economics later" is the opposite of what built every company on this list

Educational Note Of The Day Why "first hour reversals" happen so often after big gap moves When markets gap up significantly at the open (like NQ +1.6% yesterday), the first hour of cash trading frequently sees a reversal or significant pullback. Here's why: 1. Overnight gaps come from futures, not real volume.A gap up of 200+ NQ points is built on relatively thin overnight liquidity. When New York opens at 9:30 AM ET, you suddenly have institutional desks, ETF rebalancing, options market makers, and retail flow ALL hitting the tape at once. The thin gap meets thick volume — and the gap often gets challenged. 2. Gap fade is a real strategy.There are entire institutional desks built around fading opening gaps. The data supports them: roughly 60-65% of gap-ups above 1% see at least a partial fill in the first 60 minutes of cash trading. 3. Overnight news has time to be re-evaluated. At 5 AM CT, you reacted to Trump's tweet emotionally. By 9 AM, smarter desks have read the fine print, considered Iran's official response, checked oil's behavior, and decided whether to chase or fade. That reassessment process IS the morning reversal. The trading framework: Strong gap + strong volume on the open + holds above pre-market high in first 5 minutes = trend day up, lean long Strong gap + weak volume on the open + immediately rejects pre-market high = fade likely, lean short the bounce Strong gap + chop in first 15 minutes = wait, no edge The lesson from yesterday's tape: the bounce held into the close, which means today's gap-up at 9:30 is starting from a stronger foundation than yesterday's was. The legal test for trade dress infringement looks at *likelihood of confusion* among relevant consumers as to source or affiliation—not whether regular Costco members recognize the Kirkland label. Lululemon argues the close similarity in design, cut, and style of the jackets, pants, and hoodies could still lead some shoppers (newer customers, online viewers, or those less brand-savvy) to mistakenly link the cheaper Kirkland versions to Lululemon or assume they're authentic equivalents from the same makers. Costco regulars knowing the difference strengthens Costco's defense, but it doesn't erase the claim if broader evidence of potential confusion exists. Courts weigh multiple factors like product similarity and marketing channels.

I used to hear people say that in developed countries, things often cost the same number as they do in China, just in a different currency. I never really understood what they meant, but after moving to Australia, I’ve realized that it’s often true. IKEA delivery costs 89 yuan in China—and 89 Australian dollars here. When ordering groceries online, a shopping bag might cost 2 yuan in China—and 2 dollars here. A bus ride costs a few yuan in China—and 2.80 dollars here. A bottle of Coke from a convenience store costs around 4 yuan in China—and about 4 dollars here. A normal taxi ride in China might cost anywhere from the teens to just over 30 yuan. In Australia, it’s often roughly the same number in Australian dollars. One Australian dollar is about 4.72 yuan. The minimum hourly wage in Australia is around 26 dollars, while in Shanghai it’s around 25 yuan. An ordinary person here might earn a little over 4,000 Australian dollars a month, which is numerically similar to what some people earn in parts of China. The main difference is that almost anything involving human labour is very expensive in Australia, while mass-produced goods are genuinely cheap relative to local incomes. An ordinary person might earn over 4,000 dollars a month, but the latest iPhone only costs around one or two thousand—roughly half a month’s salary. Groceries such as meat, eggs and dairy cost about the same number as they do in Shanghai, but to me, the quality often feels better than what I used to buy from Hema or Dingdong. The eggs here are especially good. Fruit and vegetable prices depend on the category. Some are similar to Shanghai, while others are extremely expensive. A coffee in Shanghai costs around 25–30 yuan. Here, it costs around 5–7 Australian dollars. Again, the number is fairly similar, but relative to Australian wages, coffee is incredibly cheap. Eating out is another story. A simple meal costs around 15–20 dollars. Converted into yuan, that’s about 70–95 yuan, which feels very expensive. I haven’t had much experience yet with home repairs, cleaning services or healthcare, but I assume anything involving professional labour will be extremely expensive. So far, I’ve found two things that are cheaper than in China. The first is milk. It’s not only cheaper, but noticeably better-tasting. The second is Lululemon. Something that costs around 1,000 yuan in China might cost the equivalent of only 600–700 yuan here. I’m sure there are more. I’ll keep looking.

Anybody can shoplift in California- Proposition 47 (2014) raised the felony theft threshold from $400 to $950 and created the specific misdemeanor shoplifting statute, aiming to reduce incarceration for low-level property crimes. Rising organized retail theft and smash-and-grab incidents led voters to pass Proposition 36 in November 2024 and the Legislature to enact a bipartisan package of laws effective in 2025 that restored stronger tools against repeat offenders and organized rings while leaving ordinary first-time low-value shoplifting as a misdemeanor. Enforcement and charging decisions still vary by county and district attorney. First-time cases frequently resolve through diversion, deferred entry of judgment, civil compromise, or informal probation rather than jail time. A conviction can later be expunged under PC 1203.4 after successful completion of probation or sentence. Meanwhile- a clear pattern of policies, legislation, and cultural framing has made intervening against shoplifters professionally and socially risky for ordinary retail workers. Corporate “Observe and Report” Policies Major retailers (Walmart, Target, Lululemon, Circle K, Dollar General, and many others) maintain strict “do not confront / do not chase / do not touch” rules for non-security staff. Employees who physically intervene, follow thieves out of the store, or even engage verbally can be—and have been—fired. Notable examples: • Lululemon fired two Georgia employees in 2023 after they engaged suspected robbers (one filmed the incident). The CEO publicly defended the firings, stating employees put themselves and others “in harm’s way” and that “it’s only merchandise.” • A long-time Circle K clerk in Colorado was fired for confronting a knife-wielding shoplifter under the company’s “Don’t Confront and Chase” policy; she later sued. • Similar firings and discipline have occurred at Walmart and other chains. Companies cite legitimate concerns: employee injury or death, civil liability if force is used, and insurance costs. The practical effect is that most frontline workers are instructed to watch, call loss prevention or police, and let the merchandise walk. California Legislative Angle In 2023, the California Senate passed SB 553 (Sen. Dave Cortese), signed by Governor Newsom and effective July 1, 2024. The law requires employers to create workplace violence prevention plans and prohibits them from requiring employees to confront active shoplifters or active threats. It does not make voluntary intervention illegal, but critics (including the California Retailers Association) argued it further discourages any intervention and signals that confrontation is treated primarily as a worker-safety hazard rather than a legitimate defense of property. Cultural and Media Framing Some progressive commentary and advocacy groups frame physical intervention by store employees or security as disproportionate, potentially racist, or an escalation of violence. Narratives often emphasize: • “It’s only merchandise” (insured and replaceable). • Claims that retail theft is exaggerated or over-sensationalized. • Scrutiny of force used by loss-prevention staff, especially in cases involving demographic differences between the employee/security and the suspect. Viral videos of employees stopping thieves sometimes trigger online pile-ons accusing the worker of vigilantism, aggression, or racial profiling. At the same time, many ordinary people and polls show majority support for employees who try to stop theft and opposition to companies punishing them. Legal Reality vs. Practical Reality California still recognizes shopkeeper’s privilege (Penal Code § 490.5). Merchants and their employees may detain a person for a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner if they have probable cause the person is shoplifting. Nike and Lululemon both got sued this week for fake discounts, a "was" price the product barely sold at. The lawsuit is the cheap part. What a permanent discount actually costs you is the expensive one. A quick caveat: these are allegations, not verdicts, and both will argue their pricing was lawful. But the mechanism I care about does not care who wins in court. A discount that never turns off is not a promotion. It is a training program. The first time a customer sees "$98, now $59," the $98 does the work. The tenth time, they learn the only number that was ever real is $59, and your full price is fiction. That trains a specific customer to your brand. Discount-native, lowest lifetime value, least loyal, first to leave the moment someone else is a dollar cheaper. Your front-end ROAS looks great because cheap converts. Your repeat rate quietly erodes, and the soft P&L shows up two quarters later with no single decision to blame. It costs you at the exit too. Any serious buyer runs cohort analysis in diligence, and revenue that rides on an always-on markdown gets haircut in the multiple. And it moves your floor. A permanent discount is a permanent margin cut, so your break-even MER relocates to a worse number and never comes back down, while most brands leave their ROAS targets exactly where they were. The uncomfortable part. If your product only converts with a fake anchor next to it, that is not a pricing tactic. It is an offer problem wearing a creative costume, and no amount of ad testing fixes it. Two questions for your own site. Did the product actually sell at the "was" price in the last 90 days? And what is the always-on version of this sale teaching the people it brings you? Full breakdown in today's article.

No wonder you’re an addict!” Etc. Instead he slides into ‘boring suggestion’ mode (“Well, have you tried the one over there?”). If she has, you’re giving her old news; if she hasn’t, but she wants to CONNECT, not get matcha shop recommendations, you’re just veering off topic. Keep the conversation PERSONAL; do not slide into “helpful recommendation mode”! He partway recovers by saying she looks like she shops around here and that she “looks bougie.” This is his first real tease at her, and she laughs. Good sign! 🆇 However, he runs out of things to talk about with her and returns to the earlier open loop about what she’s out to do, asking if she’s getting Lululemon. This topic is boring and makes it feel like the conversation is ending, because rather than opening new, fun loops he is returning to the earlier, boring one he’d thread-cut away from. At this point, you notice she’s nodding her head in a more polite fashion and has stopped brushing her hair back. She feels like the conversation is nearing a natural end. She was interested earlier, but that interest has faded. The secret handshake thing is kind of neutral. This kind of touch/compliance is GOOD, however when he does it there’s not really a good reason for doing it. “Every time I see you we’re going to do this” makes it sound like they’re about to part ways but maybe they’ll see each other in the mall now and then and do the ‘secret handshake’. This is not really the frame you want… this guy needs to be closing here. He interrupts this though to take her hand and ask about her ring. That’s good! Getting some more touch, holding her hand. He actually lets her hand go (should’ve just kept holding it till she took it away or slackened up), but when she extended it toward him again he didn’t hesitate and took it right away. Good! Yet, once again, he released her hand within seconds I guess this guy doesn’t really like holding women’s hands… (She offered her hand one final time, but that time he did not take it and she brought it back down to her side in defeat.) At this point, after the dying conversation and the half-hearted hand-holding (plus him ignoring when she offered her hand again), she’s now thanking him again, as if he is just being nice/polite, and has switched to holding her hands, drink, and shopping bag in front of her body. People place barriers in front of themselves when they’re trying to create space with you, and that’s what she’s doing here. 🆇 Then he makes another mistake: at what is the lowest point of the interaction — after some boring “the conversation is circling the drain” topics, the misfires on the ‘secret handshake’ (wrong frame was set here) and holding her hand (should’ve kept holding that hand, brother), her now holding things in front of herself defensively — that is the moment he goes for the contact close. You do not want to ask girls out on low points! Ask them out on HIGH points! He needed to keep talking to her and get her back laughing and giving him open body language again, back to another high point, then ask her out. Instead, he asks out at a low point and gets “Yeah, I’ll think about it” He says they can “get matcha maybe”, which calls back the best topic they had from earlier. Not bad. However, he need to TIE THIS INTO why the two of them should hang out. Instead, he just made an ambiguous comment, and then she started giving him recommendations. ROOM FOR IMPROVEMENT: tie it to why she needs to come out with you. Tell her you’re on a ‘matcha quest’ and you need her discerning tastebuds, for instance. Find a way to make it FUN and create another high point! She needs to be excited to see you! 🆇 He responds to her recommendations by telling her “That’s too healthy for me.” I know what he’s going for — he wants to sound ‘cool’ and ‘edgy’. I used to do this all the time. However, to a person who is health-conscious, talking about how you don’t care about health does not make it sound like you are “living dangerously”, it just makes it sound like you don’t care about what she cares about and are on a totally separate wavelength. He creates a lot of DISSIMILARITY here. She’s now just nodding politely and trying to reason with him “Well Matcha-Naro (or whatever she said) is healthy!” 🆇 He then digs his hole deeper still by qualifying himself, saying he’s “trying to be more healthy”, then talks about “a fatass person”, which comes across like he’s self-deprecating… which you really only want to do when the girl is acting intimidated by your value, not when you are in catch-up mode like this guy is. She ends up trying to reassure him that he’s not fat, and then he has to clarify. These two are now completely out-of-sync. And now, if he wasn’t cooked before, he certainly is at this point At this point, she starts body-rocking (leaning back) and moves her right foot away from him as she turns to the side. She’s trying to exit this conversation. She gives him some helpful recommendations for how to keep his weight down. Very nice of her, but there’s nothing romantic here at all. 🆇 For some reason, he continues digging the dissimilarity hole even deeper, talking about how “she is different” because she is “smaller”, dismissing her advice, making her feel like they connect even less. In the end, our hero managed to turn a disinterested girl into an interested one, but then lose her interest just as quickly by slipping into “fact finding”, “recommendation sharing”, and “edgy dissimilarity.” I’ll leave you with a few takeaways to improve your own approaches: • If you feel yourself about to ask a girl about some ‘fact’, stop and think about a way to PERSONALIZE it. Ask her opinion, ask her motivation, ask for something about HER, not her ‘facts’. You don’t actually care about her facts, and she knows it. If you’re interested in her, though, you WILL care about HER (her thinking, feeling, experiences). • If you feel tempted to give her a recommendation, stop and, once again, find some way to personalize the conversation, rather than ‘recommend’. She doesn’t need your recommendations. She has friends and Yelp for that. She’s talking to you to explore a potential romantic connection, not exchange factual information and store recommendations. • If you feel tempted to ‘display your edginess’ by differing with her, just remember that TRUST before sex is primarily build through establishing similar ATTITUDES. Every time you show her you are so edgy that you and her are totally different, trust goes down, she finds it more difficult to connect with you, and the connection moves backwards. If you don’t connect with something she is saying, just CHANGE the topic, rather than try to be EDGY. It takes practice, but once you get this stuff down you can take girls who are even dismissive at first like this one was and suck them into conversations they are really enjoying, feeling attracted, and flirting in.

If you’re early in business and not yet large, don’t feel bad. The things all great builders have? Time in the game. All the greats are honest about it. Nike, ~15 years to $100M (founded as Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964, crossed $100M around fiscal 1979). Phil Knight ran the mile at Oregon, then did his Stanford MBA, where he wrote a paper arguing Japanese running shoes could do to Adidas what Japanese cameras did to Leica. Twelve years of running and thinking about running before founding day. His co-founder Bill Bowerman was his old Oregon coach, sixteen years into coaching at the school, already a legend for hand-cobbling shoes for his runners and obsessively re-soling Tigers in his garage. Bowerman had been thinking about shoe construction for two decades by the time they shook hands. Please read Show Dog. It’s a foundational book for me on entrepreneurship. Starbucks, ~22 years (founded 1971, crossed $100M around 1993). The original three (Jerry Baldwin, Zev Siegl, Gordon Bowker) were a teacher, a teacher, and a writer. They’d been roasting and selling beans for fifteen years before the company really moved. The sprint belongs to Howard Schultz, and he wasn’t a coffee guy either. Brooklyn public housing kid, football scholarship to Northern Michigan, three grinding years selling word processors at Xerox door-to-door, then five years at Hammarplast selling Swedish kitchenware (which is how he stumbled onto Starbucks as a customer). Apple, ~4 years (founded April 1976, $118M in the fiscal year ending September 1980). Wozniak, 25, had been designing circuits since he was 11. He’d been at HP for a few years building calculators, but more importantly he’d spent every Wednesday at the Homebrew Computer Club showing his designs to other obsessives. Roughly fifteen years of self-taught hardware work. Jobs, 21, was the green one: Reed dropout, a few months at Atari, a trip to India. Lululemon, ~7-8 years (founded 1998, crossed $100M in fiscal 2006). Chip Wilson, 42 at founding, had nineteen years in technical apparel behind him. He’d started Westbeach in 1979 making surf shorts, watched the surf market die, pivoted to skate, watched that fade, pivoted to snowboard outerwear, built it to ~$15M, and sold in 1997. He was already a seasoned operator before lululemon Feastables (MrBeast), $33M year one, $96M year two, $250M year three. Jimmy started uploading at 13 under MrBeast6000, mostly Minecraft and Call of Duty commentary. He spent five years uploading to nobody, dropped out of community college, until “I counted to 100,000” broke through in 2017.
